The lower trailing coat at image RIGHT already has several large ragged pale cutouts and missing edge sections. Beat2 is supposed to create the distinctive triangular tear, so a clean before-state is not established. This is visible initial-state contamination, not mere surface grain.

The sword is continuous in the far extended hand behind her body. That arm appears to come from the anatomical LEFT/far shoulder, while the nearer arm sits beside the raised knee; torso twist and occlusion limit certainty. Required RIGHT-hand ownership is not securely established.

The broad planted ivory support has finger-like digits and layered joints, matching the newly allowed construction. Black strands run from it across lit stone and meet/overlap a curved darker connection from the petal body. The exposed dark route is visible, but its exact single load-bearing junction remains less clear than the overall claw/ground relation.

Floor is broad and mostly calm, with subordinate grain. Petal veins, hair strands and fine foliage remain dense, especially behind the dark tendon; surface-only cleanup could help after state/laterality adjudication. It cannot fix the premature tear.

No separated tendon ends or fold are introduced, so the cut consequence is not prematurely completed. The shifted blade overlaps the dark route and makes an investigative probe plausible, but is less literally a withdrawn estoc after the failed ivory strike. Black petals/veins and foliage remain dense; floor grain is less dominant. A finish can expose the existing gap and limbs but cannot fix side/construction continuity.

Standing Mael returns the estoc to his right hand; torn coat and collapsed floor-level mask provide readable cost and outcome. Distant dark petal/mask silhouette appears in the left doorway. Strong elegant adult identity and horror staging. This does not resolve the third panel’s left-hand weapon swap or changing limb construction. Fine mask crack web, petal veins and glossy floor grain compete with the quiet composition.

Strong warm opaque-painted adult strain and grounded wide stance; two hands enclose one cleaver hilt, whose blade reaches the jaw/tusk area. Complete beast torso and canal at RIGHT/trees LEFT give a clear bracing foundation.

Warm face and copper/green creature identity remain appealing. Many rust chips, fine foliage and ground paint marks compete; a later faithful finish could quiet interiors without replacing the opaque painting.

The extra central underbelly leg is removed. Four coherent supports remain: two front and two rear, with visible clearance beneath the torso. Large planted near forefoot, full copper/green boar and right canal preserve the bracing scene.

Adult face, both cleaver grips, blade/jaw relationship, grounded boots, opaque warm painting and left orange-tree/right canal geography remain. No major new support or ownership regression is visible.

They do not visibly align into one straight continuous shaft. The contact also has a terminal-looking collar rather than an obvious uninterrupted middle section.
Fine armor and floor marks remain, but faces and impact dominate. This is a strong acting/cost image with a material weapon-construction concern, not an overall action failure.

Yet the second shot has offset shaft sections, the reversal does not clearly transmit force into the chest, and damage spreads between arms/upper arm. Cyan saber is still prominent afterward. Attractive acting and useful camera variation do not establish complete choreography.

The looming claw, low dodge, visible cut ends and floor-level mask make the broad horror-rule outcome understandable without captions. Foreground/portrait/wide/aftermath scale changes work, and calm finishing preserves monochrome elegance. The finer rule remains less secure: sword hand swaps in beat three then returns, limb construction shifts, and exact cut-to-specific-joint collapse is not demonstrated. Distant doorway silhouette is subtle at phone size; its presence is not a new attack.

Brace, slip toward canal, inward effort with folded support, then sitting beside a downed machine form the most tactile weight-and-fatigue arc among these three. Faces, warm opaque paint, canal-right geography and cleaver remain recognizable. The cracked-arm linkage in beat two is awkward, beat three does not fully roll the boar, and the large damaged plate changes location in the aftermath. Fine noise is reduced, but repeated broad leaf-shadow patches keep the floor comparatively active.
